what: Transocean owns offshore drilling rigs. It operates the floating vessels that drill oil and gas wells in deep water — some of the largest and most capable rigs in existence — and leases them with crews to oil companies at a daily rate.
customers: International and national oil companies drilling offshore, in deep water off Brazil, West Africa, the Gulf of Mexico, Norway and elsewhere.
money: Daily rates charged for drilling rigs and crews, under contracts lasting months to years.
moat: The most capable deepwater drillships are enormously expensive, take years to build, and very few exist. Nobody has ordered new ones in a decade because the last building cycle bankrupted much of the industry, so the supply of high-specification rigs is effectively fixed while deepwater drilling recovers. Transocean owns a large share of the best ones.
risks: Debt of $5.8B against $620.0M of cash is enormous and has repeatedly been the industry’s undoing — Transocean’s peers have been through bankruptcy and so has much of the sector.
Last year’s results showed a 73.5% net loss margin, which shows how severe the downturns are.
Day rates depend entirely on oil company exploration budgets, which are decided annually and cut quickly.
A rig without a contract earns nothing while still costing money to maintain, so utilisation is everything.
Twelve analysts average a $6.56 target against a $4.77 price, a 38% gap reflecting different views on the cycle.
opportunities: Revenue has grown every year, from $2.6B in 2021 to $4.0B in 2025, as deepwater activity recovered.
Free cash flow of $800.0M against a $5.3B market value is a 15% yield, and the shares trade at about 6.7 times free cash flow.
No new high-specification drillships have been ordered in a decade, so supply is fixed while demand recovers.
Deepwater projects have long lives and low decline rates, which makes them attractive to oil companies planning decades ahead.
Trailing net income of $292.0M marks a return to profitability after years of losses.
watch: Day rates and fleet utilisation. An offshore driller’s economics are rigs working multiplied by what they earn each day, and both are disclosed contract by contract.
view: Offshore drilling is the most violently cyclical business in energy and possibly in any industry, and the reason is the asset. A high-specification drillship costs several hundred million dollars, takes years to build, and earns nothing at all if it has no contract while still costing money to maintain. During the last boom the industry ordered far too many, the oil price fell, and most of the sector went through bankruptcy. Transocean survived with a great deal of debt attached.

The consequence of that destruction is the current opportunity. Nobody has ordered a new high-specification drillship in roughly a decade, because no lender will finance one and no board will approve it. So the supply of capable deepwater rigs is fixed, and it is slowly shrinking as older units are scrapped. Meanwhile deepwater drilling has recovered — oil companies want long-life, low-decline projects — and revenue has grown every year from $2.6 billion to $4.0 billion.

Fixed supply meeting recovering demand is exactly the setup that produces very high day rates, and the early evidence is there: $800 million of free cash flow, a 15% yield on the market value, and a return to profitability after years of losses. That is the bull case and it is a sound one.

The reason the shares are at $4.77 rather than considerably higher is $5.8 billion of debt against $620 million of cash. That debt is larger than the market value, which means the equity is a thin sliver on top of a much bigger claim — enormous upside if day rates stay strong and the debt gets paid down, and very little left if the cycle turns before it does. Last year’s 73.5% net loss margin is what the downside looks like. This is a leveraged option on deepwater day rates rather than an investment in a business, and it should be sized as one. Day rates and utilisation are the only numbers.
bull: Fixed drillship supply meets recovering deepwater demand, day rates stay high, and debt paydown transfers an enormous amount of value to a thin equity sliver.
bear: Oil companies cut exploration budgets, utilisation falls, and $5.8 billion of debt exceeding the market value leaves the equity worth very little.
